title: Choose the FIRE Path Your Life Can Fund
meta_description: Compare Coast, Barista and Fat FIRE using spending, growth, work income, healthcare, bridge access, taxes, sequence risk and decision gates.

sections.heading: Coast, Barista and Fat FIRE Solve Different Funding Problems
paragraphs: The opening photograph shows cash, a calculator, documents and a laptop. That is where every FIRE label must begin: with a funded spending plan, not an identity. Coast, Barista and Fat FIRE describe different relationships between invested assets, future work and lifestyle costs; none guarantees independence.

Coast FIRE generally means current retirement assets may grow toward a future target without further retirement contributions, assuming time and returns cooperate. The person still earns enough to cover current life. Barista FIRE adds ongoing earned income—often part time—to reduce withdrawals or provide benefits. Fat FIRE targets a higher-spending retirement with greater margin or choice.

These labels overlap. A person can coast while working part time, or pursue a high future budget while keeping consulting income. Define the funding job before choosing the label: stop contributions, leave full-time work, preserve health coverage, support family, travel extensively or create a wider safety margin.

Financial independence is not merely leaving a job. It requires resources and systems that can support spending, tax, insurance and shocks without employment income the plan assumed was gone. A portfolio number alone omits timing, access and risk.

Write the intended transition date, future work, annual spending in today’s money, location, dependants and non-portfolio income. If these are unknown, use ranges. Precision in the final balance cannot repair vagueness in the life being funded.

Treat every calculation as a scenario rather than permission to resign. Market returns vary, inflation surprises, tax rules change and health or care needs intervene. The decision needs buffers, fallback work and review dates as well as an attractive projection.

Set the comparison on one sheet. Show current age, transition age, full retirement age, present assets, annual contributions, spending floor, chosen spending, work income and verified benefits for each path. Using the same inputs prevents the Coast case from receiving optimistic returns while the Fat case receives conservative inflation. The label should change the cash-flow structure, not the honesty of the assumptions.

sections.heading: Price the Life Before Naming the FIRE Version
paragraphs: Build a present spending baseline from twelve months of actual transactions, then separate costs likely to continue, disappear or begin after work changes. Commuting may fall while travel, health insurance and daytime leisure rise. Do not multiply one unusually cheap month by twelve.

Create essential, chosen and expandable layers. Essential covers housing, food, utilities, transport, tax, insurance and health. Chosen covers valued commitments such as travel, hobbies and gifts. Expandable spending can be reduced in a bad market without threatening safety.

Include irregular costs through annual sinking amounts: home and vehicle replacement, dental work, technology, family support, legal documents and major trips. A smooth monthly budget can conceal obligations that arrive every few years.

Model housing deliberately. Mortgage payoff may lower required cash flow but property tax, service charges, repairs and insurance remain. Renting creates flexibility and renewal risk. Relocation can change tax, currency, healthcare and social support.

Value unpaid work and benefits currently supplied by an employer: health cover, disability insurance, retirement match, paid leave, equipment and professional development. Replacing them can cost more than the visible premium or contribution.

Name what a high-spending target buys. Fat FIRE is not a moral category; it may fund business-class travel, multiple homes, private healthcare, generous gifts or simply a large margin. Costs must be explicit enough to cut, insure or fund.

Price time as well as consumption. A lower-spending path may buy autonomy sooner; a higher-spending path may justify additional years of satisfying work. Record hours, commute, stress, family time and health alongside money. A choice that maximises the portfolio while exhausting the person before transition is not obviously the richer outcome.

Create a location scenario when relocation is part of the plan. Include visa, language, travel home, rent renewals, local tax, healthcare access and currency movement. A lower advertised cost of living may require private insurance, frequent flights or imported support. Test living there before assigning permanent savings to a place known only through holidays or online budgets.

sections.heading: Calculate Coast FIRE Backward From a Future Need
paragraphs: A Coast calculation asks how much invested today might grow into a required future balance without additional contributions. The formula needs a future spending target, retirement date, withdrawal framework, expected real return, fees, tax and current investable assets.

Work in today’s purchasing power with a real return, or future currency with nominal return and explicit inflation. Do not mix them. A target of £40,000 today is not the same as £40,000 thirty years from now.

Use multiple real-return assumptions rather than a single historical average. A lower return sharply raises the current balance needed to coast, especially when the date is near. The SEC’s [[S1|compound-interest calculator]] can illustrate growth, but a smooth result is not a forecast.

Separate retirement spending from the withdrawal rate used to translate spending into a target portfolio. A rule of thumb such as multiplying annual spending by 25 embeds assumptions about horizon and future returns. Test longer retirement, fees, tax, poor early markets and changing spending.

Subtract reliable income only in the years it is expected. State pensions, Social Security, annuities and rental income have start dates, tax treatment and uncertainty. Do not capitalise a benefit as though it begins on the day work stops.

A Coast threshold is conditional: ‘on track if contributions stop under these assumptions.’ It does not mean the money can be spent today. Keep the retirement assets invested and protected from withdrawals unless the plan is recalculated.

Calculate the funded ratio at several dates rather than celebrating the first day it crosses 100 percent. Markets can lift a balance above the line temporarily. Require a review using updated spending, pension estimates and asset allocation before changing contributions. Consider a confirmation period when the decision would be difficult to reverse.

sections.heading: Stress-Test the Coast Assumption Before Reducing Contributions
paragraphs: Coasting shifts risk from future contributions to time and market returns. Once contributions fall, there is less new money to buy assets during downturns and less room to correct a weak decade. The psychological relief of reaching Coast should not hide this trade-off.

Run delayed-retirement and lower-return cases. Add a contribution-resume trigger if the funded ratio falls below a chosen level. A rule written now is easier to follow than deciding during a market decline whether the plan has failed.

Consider what replaces contributions. Redirecting cash to emergency reserves, debt, childcare, education or health can improve the total plan. Allowing lifestyle costs to absorb every former contribution can make resuming saving politically difficult.

Preserve access to employer match or tax incentives where valuable. Coast is not necessarily zero contribution. A modest amount can maintain benefits, reduce risk and protect the habit at a much lower cost than rebuilding later.

Check asset allocation. A person decades from withdrawals may hold growth assets, but risk capacity also depends on job stability, debt and reaction to losses. Coast status is not permission to take more risk to force the projection.

Review annually and after job, family, residence or tax changes. If the future target rises or expected pension falls, the Coast balance changes. A milestone is useful only when it stays connected to the underlying life.

Check contribution room that may be lost. Some tax-advantaged limits are annual and cannot be recovered later, while employer matches disappear with the job. Reducing contributions can still be correct, but the plan should price the foregone subsidy and future flexibility rather than treating the cash released today as costless.

sections.heading: Barista FIRE Is a Work-and-Withdrawal Design
paragraphs: The midpoint photograph shows espresso being prepared on a commercial coffee machine. It makes the Barista label literal, but the plan does not require café work. It means chosen ongoing income reduces the amount the portfolio must supply during a transition or indefinitely.

Define job characteristics before assuming income: hours, schedule control, physical demands, travel, seasonality, benefits, training, tax and probability the work remains available. Part-time work can be less flexible than a high-paying role reduced by one day per week.

Calculate net contribution, not gross wage. Subtract commuting, meals, childcare, equipment, payroll tax, lost benefits and any health-cover cost. A lower-stress role can still be worthwhile, but the bridge amount must be honest.

Separate income required for essentials from income used for chosen spending. If all housing and health costs depend on wages, the plan is not resilient to illness or job loss. Maintain cash and insurance for a work interruption.

Model whether earnings reduce benefits, pension contributions or tax credits. Interaction rules differ by jurisdiction and household. Use official calculators and qualified advice rather than assuming each extra unit of gross pay becomes spendable cash.

Set an exit condition. Ongoing work may be satisfying, but Barista FIRE should state when portfolio funding becomes sufficient, when benefits begin or when health and care duties justify stopping. Without a review date, a temporary bridge can become an indefinite obligation.

Barista work should have a role beyond producing a round number. It may provide social contact, structure, health cover, a visa condition or a bridge that lets investments remain untouched. Rank these benefits and identify substitutes. If insurance is the main purpose, one job with unreliable eligibility may be a fragile single point of failure.

sections.heading: Make Part-Time Income Survive Real Employment Conditions
paragraphs: Test three wage cases: expected hours, half the expected hours and zero hours for a year. Seasonal businesses, caregiving and local labour markets can interrupt work. The portfolio and cash reserve should show how each case is handled.

Distinguish employee work from self-employment. Freelancing brings invoicing delays, business expenses, tax administration, insurance and income volatility. Price unpaid marketing and leave when estimating the effective hourly rate.

Benefits can be more valuable than wages, but verify eligibility, employee contribution, waiting period and continuation after hours fall. In the United States, health coverage deserves explicit analysis; in public systems, prescriptions, dental, care and private cover can still matter.

Protect employability without turning the plan into constant hustle. Keep licences, references, basic technology and a modest training budget where they preserve options. The goal is chosen work, not dependence on an optimistic gig-income estimate.

Avoid counting a hobby business at full revenue before it has a track record. Use net income after platform fees, materials, refunds and tax, and discount uncertain demand. A passion can remain valuable even when it is not a reliable bridge.

Decide who bears the income risk in a couple. One partner’s part-time work should not quietly subsidise another’s retirement without agreement. Record hours, household labour, benefits and stop conditions together.

Keep a separate business runway for self-employment. Do not use the household emergency reserve to fund inventory, marketing or clients who pay late. A service business may need professional insurance, data protection and contracts. The bridge model should show household net cash only after the business has met its own costs and tax reserves.

Model the value of flexibility in hours. A role paying less per hour may be superior if shifts can stop during caregiving or travel, while a higher wage with rigid scheduling may recreate the original constraint. Confirm cancellation rules, minimum availability and notice periods; “part time” describes hours, not necessarily control.

sections.heading: Fat FIRE Requires a Larger Margin, Not Just a Larger Number
paragraphs: The late photograph shows an older couple travelling beside a luxury convertible on the coast. It communicates the optional lifestyle often associated with Fat FIRE: costly travel, comfort and choice. The planning challenge is to distinguish durable priorities from an image that expands whenever wealth rises.

Build the target from activities and obligations rather than applying a prestige multiplier. Price home, travel, vehicles, private healthcare, family support, philanthropy, staffing and taxes separately. State which costs are fixed and which can contract after a bad year.

A larger portfolio can still be fragile if spending is inflexible, concentrated assets fund it or several homes create large maintenance obligations. Margin comes from liquidity, diversification, insurance and cuttable expenses, not from the headline balance alone.

Model lifestyle inflation before retirement. Premium travel, club memberships and property costs may rise faster than broad consumer inflation. Use category-specific assumptions where the difference is material.

Plan administration. Complex assets, trusts, companies, cross-border property and large gifts require legal, tax and operational work. Budget professional fees and document who can act during incapacity.

Define enough. If every portfolio rise creates a larger lifestyle target, the finish line recedes indefinitely. Choose the funded life, a reserve and any legacy goal; then decide what additional work is for rather than calling all accumulation necessary.

Test expensive choices independently. A second home, frequent premium flights or large family gifts may each require a specific capital amount and operating budget. Keeping them as separate modules makes it possible to delay one goal without declaring the entire Fat FIRE plan a failure. It also reveals which luxury creates the most lasting value.

sections.heading: Model Spending as a Path, Not a Flat Line
paragraphs: Retirement spending often changes. Early years may contain travel and projects, middle years may slow, and later years can bring care costs. A flat inflation-adjusted amount is a useful baseline, not a complete prediction.

Create phases with dates and drivers: bridge years before pension, active years, stable years and care contingency. Place large one-time goals in the relevant phase instead of hiding them in a permanent annual amount.

Use floor-and-flex rules. Essential spending receives the strongest funding; chosen spending can pause after poor returns; expandable spending grows only when portfolio conditions permit. This makes adjustment specific rather than asking the household to ‘be flexible’ during stress.

Budget tax separately from consumption. Withdrawals from taxable, tax-deferred and tax-free accounts can create different liabilities. Gross portfolio distribution is not the same as spendable income.

Include support for parents, adult children or charities only after agreeing amount, duration and priority. Open-ended promises can convert a flexible budget into a fixed obligation. Preserve a process for genuine emergencies.

Review actual spending annually. Compare categories and life satisfaction, then update the next phase. Do not use one expensive year to justify permanent inflation or one quiet year to underfund future activity.

Use a replacement calendar for roofs, cars, appliances and technology. Allocate each item by estimated year and cost rather than adding a vague contingency percentage. The calendar will be imperfect, but it exposes clusters of large outlays and supports a cash plan that does not depend on selling equities in a weak market.

sections.heading: Fund the Bridge Between Work and Accessible Retirement Money
paragraphs: Early retirees may have assets that cannot be accessed freely until a specified age or condition. Map each account’s access rules, tax and penalties by year. A large retirement balance can coexist with a near-term cash-flow gap.

Build a year-by-year income map with wages, cash, taxable assets, pensions, Social Security or State Pension, annuities and required distributions. Use official age and eligibility rules current for the jurisdiction.

The U.S. [[S3|Social Security retirement planner]] and UK [[S5|State Pension forecast service]] help verify benefits, but estimates can change with earnings, claiming age and policy. Preserve source date and do not substitute a blog estimate.

Keep emergency cash distinct from the planned bridge. If three years of spending are intentionally held outside retirement accounts, a separate reserve is still needed for repair, health or family shock.

Plan account sequencing with tax advice. Selling taxable assets, converting retirement accounts or taking pension early can affect tax, benefits and future income. A lower bill this year may raise lifetime tax or reduce flexibility.

Include failure routes: return to work, reduce chosen spending, delay a large purchase, claim benefits differently or sell an asset. Specify which route comes first so a market decline does not force a chaotic decision.

Account access is both legal and practical. Verify online credentials, beneficiary designations, transfer times, settlement, withdrawal forms and bank limits before leaving payroll. Test a small transfer where appropriate. A theoretical bridge can fail if an account is restricted, documentation is outdated or only one household member understands the process.

sections.heading: Price Health, Insurance and Care Before Leaving Work
paragraphs: Health risk affects all three FIRE paths. Coast plans depend on years of earning, Barista plans may depend on work capacity or benefits, and Fat plans may include private care. Insurance must match the transition rather than disappear with employment.

List health premium, deductible or excess, prescriptions, dental, vision, travel cover and long-term care exposure. Use the rules and prices for residence, age and household, then stress-test a high-use year.

In the United States, Medicare eligibility and marketplace coverage dates create bridge issues. [[S4|Medicare’s official costs page]] provides current programme figures; employer or marketplace plans require their own documents. Do not assume ‘part time’ guarantees affordable cover.

Maintain disability and life insurance where income, dependants or debt justify it. Reaching a portfolio milestone may reduce need but does not automatically remove it. Check exclusions, inflation and end dates.

Plan care work inside the household. A partner leaving employment may provide unpaid care that would otherwise cost money, but that role can limit future earnings and retirement contributions. Record the trade-off rather than treating it as free.
Create a health-trigger review. A diagnosis, loss of cover, caregiving duty or move should reopen the transition date, work plan and spending floor before assets are committed elsewhere.

Compare insurance with self-funding explicitly. A high deductible may be manageable with a dedicated reserve; an uncapped or catastrophic exposure may not be. Review policy networks, geographical cover and renewal rules before travel or relocation. Health assumptions deserve the same documentation as expected market returns because either can change the transition date.

Do not postpone every preventive expense in pursuit of the date. Dental care, therapy, ergonomic equipment, exercise and routine screening can protect both quality of life and future earning capacity. The accumulation plan should fund current health; a larger portfolio is a poor exchange for avoidable damage created while chasing independence.

sections.heading: Stress Inflation, Tax and Sequence Together
paragraphs: Sequence risk means poor returns near the start of withdrawals can damage sustainability more than the same average returns in a different order. Coast accumulators and Barista earners face less immediate withdrawal pressure, but layoffs can turn accumulation into an unplanned draw.

Run an early bear market with high inflation and no part-time income. Reduce asset values, increase essential costs and apply tax. Single-variable sensitivity misses the way risks can arrive together.

Use conservative fees and tax drag. Fund expenses, advice, trading, platform costs and foreign withholding reduce the return available to support spending. Small annual differences compound across long horizons.

Do not apply one withdrawal percentage to every horizon and portfolio. Historical research is useful evidence, but taxes, fees, asset mix, valuations, spending flexibility and retirement length differ. A dynamic policy needs rules, not faith in one number.

Model inflation by category. Housing, health, education support and travel may not follow the headline index. Use a blended baseline and separate stress for categories that dominate the chosen FIRE version.
Document nominal and real outputs, return order and rebalance assumptions. A chart without assumptions can make a fragile plan look scientific. The model should be reproducible by another reviewer.

Run the plan through historical and synthetic sequences, but do not confuse a high success percentage with certainty. Simulation quality depends on distributions, correlations, fees and behaviour rules. Inspect failed cases: which year, expense or return caused the breach, and which pre-agreed adjustment would have been realistic for the household?

sections.heading: Build a Portfolio and Withdrawal Policy That Match the Path
paragraphs: Choose asset allocation from horizon, spending floor, flexibility and loss capacity—not from the FIRE label. A long Coast horizon may support more equity, while a person beginning withdrawals needs liquidity and sequence protection. Individual circumstances can reverse simple rules.

Define the role of cash, high-quality bonds and growth assets. Cash pays near-term commitments, bonds can stabilise planned withdrawals and equities pursue long-term growth. Each layer still carries inflation, interest-rate or market risk.

Set withdrawal order, rebalancing range and bad-market adjustments. Examples include funding essentials from cash, pausing inflation increases for chosen spending or replenishing reserves after strong markets. Test tax consequences before automating.

Avoid using high expected returns to make an unaffordable lifestyle appear funded. A more aggressive portfolio can raise upside and downside; it does not convert risk into certainty. Change date, saving, work or spending before forcing the return assumption.

Treat concentrated employer stock, property and business interests as part of the total portfolio. They may be hard to sell during the same event that ends employment. Diversification should precede dependence where tax and market conditions permit.

Write a governance page naming accounts, access, beneficiaries, decision authority and emergency contacts. Independence fails operationally if a partner cannot find assets or understand the withdrawal process.

Match portfolio complexity to the operator. A multi-bucket strategy, conversion ladder or tactical rule may look efficient but fail if records lapse or a surviving partner cannot maintain it. Prefer transparent holdings, low costs and written procedures. Professional help can be valuable when its scope, fees, credentials, custody and conflicts are understood.

sections.heading: Plan the Human Transition Out of Full-Time Work
paragraphs: Work supplies structure, relationships, identity and status as well as income. Define a weekly life before leaving: sleep, exercise, care, learning, community, creative work and unstructured time. A funded calendar can still feel empty.

Test the desired life through leave, reduced hours or a sabbatical where feasible. Observe spending, routine and relationship effects. A trial can reveal that autonomy matters more than zero work, supporting a Coast or Barista route.

Couples should agree whose work continues, who receives health or pension benefits, how household labour changes and what spending is personal. One partner’s FIRE must not become the other partner’s compulsory overtime.
Prepare an answer for returning to work. Maintain records, networks and a credible explanation without shame. Re-entry can be a rational contingency, not evidence that the experiment failed.

Set information boundaries. Announcing a retirement number can attract pressure, scams, loans and judgement. Share only what supports relationships and professional needs; protect account details and security.

Expect the transition to evolve. Some people discover meaningful paid work after reaching independence. The aim is the ability to choose under a funded plan, not loyalty to a label invented before life changed.

Plan social change without buying it. Leaving a demanding career can remove colleagues and status at the same moment free time expands. Budget trial memberships and travel cautiously, then observe which activities create durable connection. Fat spending cannot guarantee purpose, and a leaner path need not mean isolation when community is designed deliberately.

sections.heading: Choose With a Decision Gate, Then Review Annually
paragraphs: For Coast FIRE, require the current balance to meet conservative growth cases, present life to be funded by earned income, and a contribution-resume trigger. For Barista FIRE, require verified net income or a zero-income fallback. For Fat FIRE, require itemised lifestyle costs and genuine flexibility.

All paths need emergency cash, debt control, insurance, diversified assets, account access, tax review, legal documents and household agreement. A high funded ratio does not replace these operating controls.

Use a go, delay or redesign decision. Delay is correct when healthcare, bridge access, dependants or stress tests remain unresolved. Redesign may mean phased hours, a smaller lifestyle, later date or different location rather than abandoning the goal.

Write annual review inputs: actual spending, portfolio, contributions, net side income, benefits, pension estimates, tax, health, dependants and satisfaction with work. Compare with ranges instead of one brittle target.

Set immediate stop conditions for transition: job loss before reserves are ready, insurance denial, major new care duty, hidden debt, partner disagreement or a material model error. Protect optionality before protecting the announced date.

Choose the version that funds the intended life under conservative conditions and remains acceptable when work, markets or health differ from plan. Coast, Barista and Fat FIRE are useful only when they clarify the cash-flow job; the durable objective is controlled time supported by resilient resources.

Record the minimum acceptable fallback before transition. It might be twelve months of full-time work, two years of reduced travel, a later pension claim or relocation. Confirm that every adult could accept it. A fallback that exists only on a spreadsheet but violates health, family or immigration constraints is not genuine resilience.

Before giving notice, hold a final meeting using current balances rather than month-old projections. Verify the first year of income, tax withholding, insurance start dates, automatic payments and emergency contacts. Document the decision and a thirty-day administrative checklist. Celebration belongs after the transition controls are in place, not instead of them. Keep the signed version with pension, insurance and estate documents for future reviews. Review that record together before every major change.

summary: Coast, Barista and Fat FIRE describe different funding jobs. Coast assumes current retirement assets may grow without further contributions; Barista uses ongoing earned income to reduce withdrawals or provide benefits; Fat funds a higher-spending lifestyle or larger margin. The labels can overlap.

Price the life before choosing a label. Use actual annual spending, then add irregular replacement, health, tax, insurance and family costs. Separate essential, chosen and expandable layers and identify employer benefits that must be replaced.

Calculate Coast backward from future spending, retirement date and a withdrawal framework. Keep real and nominal assumptions consistent, test several returns and subtract reliable pension income only when it begins. A Coast number is conditional, not spendable cash.

Stress Coast with lower returns, delayed retirement and resumed-contribution triggers. Consider retaining employer matches or modest saving. Redirected contributions should serve explicit current goals rather than disappearing automatically into lifestyle.

Barista FIRE is a work-and-withdrawal design, not necessarily café employment. Define hours, control, benefits, durability and net income after commuting, care, tax and equipment. Test zero-income periods and set an exit condition.

Fat FIRE needs itemised lifestyle costs, category-specific inflation, liquidity, diversification and flexible expenses. A large portfolio remains fragile when costs cannot contract or concentrated assets fund several expensive obligations. Define enough so the target does not rise forever.

Model spending in phases: bridge, active, stable and care years. Protect the essential floor while allowing chosen and expandable spending to change after poor markets. Budget taxes separately from household consumption.

Map account access year by year. Retirement assets may be unavailable or costly before specified ages. Combine wages, cash, taxable investments, pensions and benefits, while keeping emergency cash separate from the planned bridge.

Price health premiums, cost sharing, dental, prescriptions, travel cover, disability, life insurance and care. Verify eligibility and benefits instead of assuming part-time work or a public programme solves every cost.

Stress poor early returns, inflation, tax and lost income together. Sequence matters once withdrawals begin. Do not use one withdrawal rate for every horizon, portfolio, fee level and spending pattern.

Build asset allocation and withdrawal rules around spending floor, flexibility and horizon. Define cash, bonds and growth roles, rebalancing, tax-aware account order and bad-market adjustments. Never raise expected return merely to make spending appear affordable.

Plan the human transition. Test reduced hours or leave, design a weekly life, preserve employability and agree household work, benefits, privacy and decision rights. Returning to work can be a contingency rather than failure.

Use a decision gate: Coast requires conservative funding and a restart trigger; Barista requires net-income evidence and a no-work fallback; Fat requires explicit costs and flexibility. Every path also needs reserves, insurance, access, tax review and agreement.

Review actual spending, assets, income, benefits, health, dependants and life satisfaction annually. Stop a transition after major funding, insurance, care, debt or household surprises. Choose the path that buys controlled time under imperfect conditions, not the most impressive label.

Compare every path on one consistent sheet containing ages, assets, contributions, spending layers, net work income and verified benefits. Include time, health and family effects. Different labels should change the funding structure, not receive different standards of evidence.

Protect practical execution. Price foregone contribution room and employer benefits, separate business and household reserves, calendar major replacements, verify account access and document insurance limits. A bridge fails if money exists on paper but cannot be accessed safely when needed.

Treat simulations as conditional evidence, not certainty. Inspect failed cases and confirm that proposed spending cuts, work or relocation are genuinely acceptable. Keep holdings and withdrawal processes simple enough for every responsible household member to operate during illness, bereavement or market stress.

faq.question: What is Coast FIRE?
faq.answer: It generally means existing retirement assets may grow toward a future target without further contributions, while earned income still funds current life. The result depends on returns, time and spending assumptions.

faq.question: Does Barista FIRE require working in a café?
faq.answer: No. It refers to ongoing earned income or benefits reducing portfolio withdrawals. The job must be modelled using net income, realistic hours and a no-work fallback.

faq.question: What makes Fat FIRE different?
faq.answer: It targets a higher-spending retirement or larger margin. The plan needs itemised lifestyle costs, category inflation, liquidity and expenses that can contract after poor markets.

faq.question: Can a person combine FIRE paths?
faq.answer: Yes. Someone can coast while working part time, or keep consulting income after funding a high-spending target. Define the portfolio and work jobs rather than defending a label.

faq.question: Is multiplying annual spending by 25 enough?
faq.answer: No. That shortcut embeds withdrawal assumptions and omits tax, fees, horizon, sequence, pensions, healthcare and spending flexibility.

faq.question: What is the biggest early-retirement blind spot?
faq.answer: Common omissions include health cover, account-access bridge years, irregular replacements, tax, care duties and the possibility that part-time income disappears.

faq.question: When should the transition be delayed?
faq.answer: Delay or redesign after unresolved insurance, bridge, debt, care, household-agreement or stress-test problems. Protecting optionality is more important than an announced date.

glossary.definition: A strategy in which current retirement assets are expected to grow toward a later target with reduced or no new contributions.
A strategy combining ongoing earned income or employment benefits with portfolio resources.
A financial-independence target designed to support comparatively high spending or a large margin.
Investment return after accounting for inflation.
Available assets divided by assets required under stated assumptions.
Years between leaving primary work and gaining practical access to pensions or other retirement income.
The risk that poor returns near withdrawals cause greater damage than the same average returns in another order.
Essential costs that the plan aims to protect before discretionary spending.
Rules for account order, amount, inflation, rebalancing and bad-market adjustments.
A predefined event that pauses or reverses a planned transition.
